Summary: Pelagianism taught in the late 4th and early 5th centuries that humans are born morally neutral and can choose good without special divine grace. It denied that Adam's sin was transmitted to his descendants as a corrupted nature.
Beliefs: Humans are born without original sin; Human will alone can achieve righteousness; Grace helps but is not necessary for salvation; Adam's sin affected only Adam
Controversy: Condemned at the Council of Carthage AD 418 and the Council of Ephesus AD 431 in the debate with Augustine
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that all people need God's grace because of a fallen nature, citing passages such as Romans 5 and Ephesians 2 on sin and grace.

Summary: Semi-Pelagianism arose in southern Gaul in the 5th century as a middle position. It taught that the first step toward faith can come from human will, with God's grace then completing what the person began.
Beliefs: Humans can initiate faith on their own; God's grace cooperates with human will after the first step; Original sin weakens but does not fully corrupt the will
Controversy: Addressed at the Second Council of Orange AD 529, which affirmed that even the beginning of faith is a gift of grace
ChristianResponse: The church taught that faith itself begins by grace, pointing to Philippians 2:13 and John 6:44, while still affirming human responsibility to respond.
RelatedPeople: John Cassian; Augustine; Prosper of Aquitaine

Summary: Arianism taught in the early 4th century that the Son of God was created by the Father and therefore not eternal or fully God. It held that there was a time when the Son did not exist.
Beliefs: Jesus Christ was created by God the Father; The Son is not eternal; The Son is divine but not fully God; The Father alone is uncreated
Controversy: Condemned at the Council of Nicaea AD 325, which produced the Nicene Creed
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that the Son is of one substance with the Father and eternally begotten, not made, citing John 1:1 and Colossians 1:15-17.

Summary: Gnosticism was a diverse movement in the 1st and 2nd centuries that taught salvation comes through secret knowledge. It often viewed the material world as evil and created by a lesser god.
Beliefs: Salvation comes through secret knowledge; The material world is evil; The God of the Old Testament is a lesser creator; Jesus brought hidden knowledge for the spiritual elite
Controversy: Opposed by early church writers such as Irenaeus in Against Heresies (c. AD 180) and by the formation of the New Testament canon
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that creation is good, salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, and the gospel is openly proclaimed, citing Genesis 1 and John 1.

Founder: Early teachers in the late 1st and 2nd centuries
Summary: Docetism taught that Jesus only seemed to have a physical body and to suffer. Its name comes from the Greek word meaning to seem or appear.
Beliefs: Jesus only appeared to be human; Christ did not truly suffer or die in the flesh; The spiritual Christ separated from the man Jesus at the cross
Controversy: Opposed in the letters of Ignatius of Antioch (c. AD 110) and addressed in 1 John and 2 John
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that Jesus came truly in the flesh and truly died and rose bodily, citing 1 John 4:2-3 and Luke 24:39.
RelatedPeople: Ignatius of Antioch; John the Apostle

Summary: Marcionism taught in the 2nd century that the God of the Old Testament was different from and inferior to the God revealed by Jesus. Marcion rejected the Old Testament and edited the New Testament writings he accepted.
Beliefs: The Old Testament God is a separate and harsh creator; The God of Jesus is only love and mercy; The Old Testament should be rejected; Only parts of Luke and Paul's letters are Scripture
Controversy: Marcion was excommunicated in Rome AD 144; his teaching prompted the church to clarify the canon of Scripture
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed one God revealed in both Testaments and preserved the Old Testament as Scripture, citing Luke 24:27 and 2 Timothy 3:16.
RelatedDoctrines: Canon of Scripture; Nature of God; Old Testament

Summary: Montanism, also called the New Prophecy, began in Phrygia in the 2nd century. It emphasized ecstatic prophecy, strict discipline, and an expectation that the New Jerusalem would soon appear in Phrygia.
Beliefs: New prophecies continue through Montanus and his followers; Ecstatic speech is a mark of the Spirit; Strict fasting and discipline are required; The end times would center on Pepuza in Phrygia
Controversy: Councils in Asia Minor in the late 2nd century rejected its prophecies; Tertullian later supported the movement
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed the work of the Holy Spirit while teaching that prophecy must be tested by Scripture and that Christ's return is not tied to one place, citing 1 Thessalonians 5:20-21.

Summary: Sabellianism, also called Modalism or Modalistic Monarchianism, taught in the 3rd century that God is one person who reveals himself in three successive modes. In this view the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not distinct persons.
Beliefs: God is one person in three modes; Father, Son, and Spirit are not distinct persons; God the Father suffered on the cross in the mode of the Son
Controversy: Condemned in Rome in the early 3rd century and opposed by Tertullian and Hippolytus; later rejected in Trinitarian creeds
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed one God in three distinct persons who coexist eternally, citing Matthew 28:19 and the baptism of Jesus in Matthew 3.

Summary: Nestorianism is associated with Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, who emphasized a distinction between Christ's divine and human natures. Critics argued his teaching divided Christ into two persons.
Beliefs: Christ's divine and human natures are loosely joined; Mary should be called Christotokos rather than Theotokos; The human and divine in Christ act as separate subjects
Controversy: Condemned at the Council of Ephesus AD 431 in the debate with Cyril of Alexandria
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that Jesus is one person with two natures, fully God and fully man, citing John 1:14 and Philippians 2.
RelatedDoctrines: Incarnation; Deity of Christ; Hypostatic Union

Summary: Monophysitism taught in the 5th century that Christ has only one nature, in which his humanity was absorbed into his divinity. Eutyches was a leading figure in the controversy.
Beliefs: Christ has one nature only; Christ's humanity was absorbed by his divinity; Christ is not fully human in the same way as other humans
Controversy: Condemned at the Council of Chalcedon AD 451, which defined Christ in two natures without confusion or separation
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that Jesus is fully God and fully man in one person, citing Hebrews 4:15 and Colossians 2:9.
RelatedDoctrines: Incarnation; Hypostatic Union; Humanity of Christ

Summary: Donatism arose in North Africa after persecution under Diocletian in the early 4th century. It taught that the church must be pure and that sacraments administered by clergy who had lapsed under persecution were invalid.
Beliefs: The church must consist only of the pure; Sacraments by unworthy clergy are invalid; Christians who lapsed under persecution must be rebaptized to rejoin
Controversy: Addressed at the Council of Arles AD 314 and in Augustine's writings; a conference at Carthage AD 411 ruled against the Donatists
ChristianResponse: The church taught that the validity of baptism and communion rests on Christ, not the moral worth of the minister, citing Matthew 13 on wheat and weeds growing together.

Summary: Manichaeism was founded by Mani in Persia in the 3rd century as a dualistic religion. It taught an eternal struggle between light and darkness and spread across the Roman and Persian worlds.
Beliefs: Good and evil are two eternal opposing powers; Matter is associated with darkness and evil; Salvation comes through knowledge that frees light trapped in matter; Mani was a final prophet
Controversy: Opposed by Christian, Zoroastrian, and later Muslim writers; Augustine, a former hearer, refuted it in the late 4th and early 5th centuries
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed one sovereign Creator and that creation was made good, citing Genesis 1 and Colossians 1:16-17.

Summary: Ebionism was held by some early Jewish-Christian groups who kept the Mosaic law as binding for all followers of Jesus. They typically viewed Jesus as a human prophet and Messiah rather than as pre-existent and divine.
Beliefs: Jesus was a human Messiah, not pre-existent God; Keeping the Mosaic law is required for salvation; Jesus was adopted as God's son because of his obedience; Paul's teaching was rejected by many Ebionites
Controversy: Opposed by writers such as Irenaeus and Origen; its views were inconsistent with the councils affirming Christ's deity
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed Jesus as Lord and God and taught justification by faith, while honoring the law's role in Israel's history, citing Acts 15 and Galatians 2-3.
RelatedDoctrines: Deity of Christ; Justification; Law and Grace

Summary: Apollinarianism taught in the 4th century that Christ had a human body and soul but that the divine Logos replaced his human mind. It sought to protect Christ's sinlessness and unity.
Beliefs: Christ had no human rational mind; The Logos took the place of Christ's human mind; Christ was not fully human in mind
Controversy: Condemned at the Council of Constantinople AD 381; Gregory of Nazianzus argued what is not assumed is not healed
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that Jesus assumed full humanity, including a human mind, to redeem the whole person, citing Hebrews 2:17 and Luke 2:52.

Summary: Socinianism developed in Poland and Transylvania in the 16th century under Fausto Sozzini, known as Socinus. It rejected the Trinity and the deity of Christ and emphasized reason in interpreting Scripture.
Beliefs: God is one person, not a Trinity; Jesus was a man, not pre-existent God; Christ's death was an example and moral influence, not a substitutionary atonement; Original sin is denied
Controversy: Debated across Reformation Europe; Socinians were expelled from Poland in 1658 and their views were opposed by Reformed and Catholic theologians
ChristianResponse: Historic churches affirmed the Trinity and Christ's atoning death, citing John 1, Matthew 28:19, and Isaiah 53.

Founder: Thinkers including Thomas Paine (1737-1809) and earlier English deists
Summary: Deism grew in the 17th and 18th centuries during the Enlightenment. It taught that God created the world but does not intervene in it through miracles, revelation, or providence.
Beliefs: God created the world and then does not intervene; Miracles and special revelation are rejected; Religion should rest on reason and nature alone; Prayer does not change God's actions
Controversy: Debated by Christian apologists in the 18th century and contrasted with biblical theism in sermons and treatises of the period
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed a God who acts in history, answers prayer, and revealed himself in Scripture and in Christ, citing Exodus, the Psalms, and Hebrews 1.
RelatedPeople: Thomas Paine; John Locke; Joseph Butler

Founder: Modern teachers and movements emphasizing human ability
Summary: This entry describes modern ideas that echo Pelagian themes, such as the belief that people are basically good and can perfect themselves by effort alone. It is included as a comparison category, not as a single historic movement.
Beliefs: People are basically good by nature; Moral improvement comes mainly from personal effort; Talk of sin and grace is unnecessary or harmful; Examples and education are enough to save
Controversy: Discussed by theologians in response to self-help and moralistic teaching in churches and popular culture
ChristianResponse: The church response emphasizes both human responsibility and the need for grace and new birth, citing Jeremiah 17:9, John 3, and Titus 3:5.

Founder: Teachers including Kenneth Hagin (1917-2003) and later Word of Faith teachers
Summary: The Prosperity Gospel, associated with the Word of Faith movement in the 20th and 21st centuries, teaches that faith, positive confession, and giving will reliably bring health and material wealth. Critics in historic churches view this as a distortion of biblical teaching on suffering and contentment.
Beliefs: Faith guarantees health and wealth in this life; Speaking positive confessions creates reality; Giving money leads to multiplied financial return; Suffering usually indicates lack of faith
Controversy: Addressed in statements and books by evangelical, Reformed, and Pentecostal leaders who affirm healing and provision while rejecting guaranteed wealth formulas
ChristianResponse: The church response affirms God's goodness and care while teaching contentment, generosity, and trust in suffering, citing Philippians 4, 1 Timothy 6, and the book of Job.

Founder: Cathar teachers in southern France (12th-13th centuries)
Summary: Albigensianism, or Catharism, flourished in southern France in the 12th and 13th centuries. It was a dualistic movement that viewed the material world as evil and taught an elite class of the perfected.
Beliefs: Matter is evil and spirit is good; The God of the Old Testament is different from the God of the New; The perfecti followed strict ascetic practices; Salvation comes through a ritual called the consolamentum
Controversy: Condemned by the Fourth Lateran Council AD 1215; followed by preaching campaigns and the Albigensian Crusade (1209-1229)
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed one good Creator and the goodness of creation and marriage, citing Genesis 1 and 1 Timothy 4, while later historians note the tragedy of violence in the response.

Summary: Jansenism was a movement within Roman Catholicism in the 17th and 18th centuries, based on Jansen's work on Augustine. It emphasized human corruption, predestination, and strict moral practice, and was opposed by Jesuit theologians and several popes.
Beliefs: Human nature is deeply corrupted without grace; Grace is irresistible for the elect; Christ died for the elect in a particular sense; Strict moral and sacramental discipline is required
Controversy: Condemned in part by Pope Innocent X in Cum Occasione AD 1653 and by Pope Clement XI in Unigenitus AD 1713
ChristianResponse: Responses varied; critics argued it understated God's universal saving will, citing 1 Timothy 2:4, while others valued its emphasis on grace and holiness.
RelatedPeople: Cornelius Jansen; Blaise Pascal; Antoine Arnauld

Summary: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints was founded by Joseph Smith in the United States in 1830. It is included here as a modern comparison entry because its teachings on God, Christ, and Scripture differ from historic Nicene Christianity, while its members describe themselves as Christians.
Beliefs: God the Father has a physical body and was once mortal in Latter-day Saint teaching; Additional Scriptures include the Book of Mormon; Continuing revelation comes through a living prophet; Humans can progress toward exaltation
Controversy: Discussed in comparative theology since the 19th century; historic churches note differences from the Nicene Creed on God and Christ
ChristianResponse: Historic churches respond by affirming the Trinity as defined at Nicaea and the sufficiency of the biblical canon, citing Deuteronomy and Revelation on adding to Scripture, while encouraging respectful dialogue.

Summary: Jehovah's Witnesses originated in the United States in the 1870s under Charles Taze Russell and were later led by Joseph Rutherford. It is included here as a modern comparison entry because its teachings on the Trinity, Christ, and the Holy Spirit differ from historic Nicene Christianity.
Beliefs: God is one person, Jehovah; Jesus is Michael the archangel and a created being; The Holy Spirit is God's active force, not a person; Only 144000 are anointed to reign in heaven in their teaching
Controversy: Discussed in comparative theology since the early 20th century; historic churches contrast its Christology with Arianism and the Nicene Creed
ChristianResponse: Historic churches affirm Jesus as fully God and the Spirit as a divine person, citing John 1, Acts 5, and Matthew 28:19, while encouraging respectful and factual conversation.
RelatedDoctrines: Trinity; Deity of Christ; Holy Spirit

Summary: Adoptionism taught in the 2nd and 8th centuries that Jesus was born a human and was adopted as God's Son at his baptism or resurrection because of his obedience. It denied his pre-existence as God the Son.
Beliefs: Jesus was adopted as Son at his baptism; Jesus did not pre-exist as God; Jesus earned sonship by obedience; Christ's deity is a conferred status, not his nature
Controversy: Condemned in Rome in the late 2nd century and again in the Spanish Adoptionist controversy addressed at Frankfurt AD 794
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that Jesus is God's Son by nature from eternity, citing John 1:1-14 and Romans 1:3-4.

Summary: Monothelitism taught in the 7th century that Christ has two natures but only one will, the divine will. It was promoted as a compromise between Chalcedonian and Monophysite positions.
Beliefs: Christ has one will only; Christ's human will did not truly operate; Unity in Christ requires a single will
Controversy: Condemned at the Third Council of Constantinople AD 680-681, which affirmed two wills in Christ
ChristianResponse: The church affirmed that Jesus has a true human will as well as a divine will, citing Luke 22:42 where Jesus prays not my will but yours be done.
RelatedPeople: Sergius I; Maximus the Confessor; Pope Martin I
RelatedDoctrines: Incarnation; Humanity of Christ; Hypostatic Union

Founder: Michael Servetus (1511-1553) and later Unitarian churches
Summary: Unitarianism, in its historic form, teaches that God is one person and denies the Trinity and the pre-existence and full deity of Christ. It developed from 16th-century anti-Trinitarian movements into organized churches in Poland, Transylvania, England, and America.
Beliefs: God is one person; Jesus was a great teacher and moral example, not God incarnate; The Holy Spirit is not a distinct divine person; Reason and conscience guide interpretation of Scripture
Controversy: Debated throughout the Reformation and Enlightenment; historic confessions such as Westminster and the Nicene Creed were written in part to affirm Trinitarian faith against it
ChristianResponse: Historic churches affirm one God in three persons and salvation through Christ's death and resurrection, citing Matthew 28:19, John 20:28, and 1 Corinthians 15.
RelatedPeople: Michael Servetus; Fausto Sozzini; Joseph Priestley
